extraction.name: MATH
extraction.description: A dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems with full step-by-step solutions written in LaTeX and natural language, designed to measure mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models across seven subjects and five difficulty levels.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.citeAs: Hendrycks, D., Burns, C., Kadavath, S., Arora, A., Basart, S., Tang, E., Song, D., & Steinhardt, J. (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from high school mathematics competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and others, accessible via Art of Problem Solving (aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests) spanning decades.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: High school math competitions (e.g., AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME) created by the Mathematical Association of America (MAA) and hosted on AoPS.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions were formatted consistently using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language for figures. Final answers are enclosed in \boxed{} and formatted using specific rules: probabilities as simplified fractions, matrix entry fractions as x/y, other fractions as \frac{x}{y}, coefficients without multiplication signs, expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order, and polynomials in decreasing degree order. Parentheses encodings and equivalent numeric representations were normalized for exact match evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Difficulty levels were tagged from 1 (easiest) to 5 (hardest) following AoPS, and categorized across seven subjects (Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus). Problems were curated from competition math sources with full step-by-step solutions and final boxed answers.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: High performance (even 40% accuracy) on this dataset by machine learning models could have ramifications for cheating on homework. The authors explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models to help students cheat on mathematics exams, but rather to forecast reasoning capabilities.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: State-of-the-art Transformer models achieve low accuracy (3.0% to 6.9%), models are highly overconfident (AUROC for detecting errors is 68.8%), and generating step-by-step solutions degrades accuracy due to compounding errors in intermediate derivations. Additionally, scaling trends suggest impractical parameter counts (10^35) would be required to reach human-level performance without new algorithmic advancements.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing, fine-tuning, and benchmarking mathematical problem-solving and reasoning capabilities of language models. Divided into 7,500 training problems and 5,000 test problems.
